extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, administrative agency policymakers, and First Amendment practitioners (lawyers advising agencies on notice-and-comment/social media moderation)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate or craft federal agency policies governing which public comments will be posted, edited, or deleted on agency websites/social media (notice-and-comment and public-facing comment forums), with attention to First Amendment constraints and doctrinal theories of free speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulgar/obscene/indecent/profane/abusive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies will not post or will delete comments that contain vulgar, obscene, indecent, profane, or abusive language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from agency policies: Commerce.gov disallows comments that “contain vulgar language.” The EPA will not post comments that “contain obscene, indecent, or profane language.” DOD bars “vulgar or abusive language.” FEMA will delete “abusive or vulgar language.” Note variation across agencies (some mention such language explicitly; others, like the SSA in this sample, do not). Consider whether a policy uses "will not post" vs. "will delete" or simply "encourages" civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive/hate/discriminatory language targeting specific demographic groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments containing offensive terms, hate speech, or discriminatory language targeted at specific ethnic, racial, or other demographic groups will be removed or not posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency-language examples: the Department of State will not post “offensive terms that target specific ethnic or racial groups.” DHS will remove comments that “contain offensive terms that target specific ethnic or racial groups.” USDA will not post comments that “include offensive language targeting specific ethnic or racial groups.” EPA will delete comments that “contain hate speech directed at race, color, sex, sexual orientation, national origin, ethnicity, age, religion, or disability.” DOD will delete comments that contain “hate speech or offensive language targeting any specific demographic.” Commerce will not post comments that contain “offensive terms that target specific ethnic or racial groups.” SSA will delete comments that contain “discriminatory language (including hate speech) based on race, national origin, age, gender, sexual orientation, religion or disability.” GSA and GAO policies similarly prohibit “offensive terms targeting individuals or groups.” Guidance: list of protected characteristics in agency texts should be observed; agencies differ in breadth of protected categories. Be careful that broadly phrased prohibitions do not amount to impermissible viewpoint discrimination under the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies will delete comments that constitute defamation directed at a person or group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The SBA will delete “defamation to a person or group of people.” Drafting guidance: specify whether allegation of defamation will be judged by a legal standard (e.g., libel) and provide a notice/appeal process to avoid chilling protected speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-topic / irrelevant / far off-topic comments (and multiple successive off-topic posts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that are off topic, irrelevant, far off-topic, or multiple successive off-topic posts by a single user may be deleted or not posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency examples: Department of State and VA will not post “off topic” comments. NASA will delete or edit “irrelevant” comments. USDA and Commerce will not post comments that “are far off-topic.” GAO will remove “[m]ultiple successive off-topic posts by a single user.” DOD, HHS, and GSA may merely encourage on-topic posting rather than enforce deletion. Guidance: policies vary from hard removal to soft encouragement; agencies should state whether they will edit, remove, or simply warn, and define "off-topic" or "irrelevant" with examples to reduce vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing (versus deleting) irrelevant or inappropriate comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Some agencies reserve the right to edit comments (rather than only delete) when comments are irrelevant or violate rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: NASA will delete or edit “irrelevant” comments. Drafting tip: agencies should state the scope of editable content (e.g., removing links, vulgar words, personally identifying information) and disclose editing practices to commenters to minimize concerns about altering substantive viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of endorsement / Establishment Clause concerns (religious speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may avoid posting or may delete comments they believe would amount to government endorsement of religion or religious beliefs; yet no sampled comment policy explicitly mentioned religion, creating potential conflict between Establishment Clause concerns and commenters' free speech/free exercise rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes: 'Intriguingly, no comment policy mentions religion or religious speech.' The government cannot endorse religion; agencies worried that leaving certain comments posted amounts to endorsement might delete such comments. Guidance: agencies must balance Establishment Clause avoid‑endorsement concerns against First Amendment protections for private religious speech and free exercise; explain rationale in policy and apply narrowly to avoid viewpoint discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment doctrinal constraints (protection for offensive/insulting speech and prohibition on viewpoint discrimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under conventional First Amendment doctrine, the Free Speech Clause protects dialogue and deliberation necessary for democracy and provides presumptive protection even for speech characterized as "offensive," "outrageous," or "insulting;" governmental restrictions that discriminate on viewpoint are unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities/examples: Cohen v. California (offensive language), Hustler Magazine v. Falwell (outrageous speech), Boos v. Barry (insulting speech), and Sons of Confederate Veterans (viewpoint discrimination on specialty license plates). Practical implication: agency moderation rules must be carefully framed and applied to avoid impermissible viewpoint discrimination; broadly worded prohibitions (e.g., "otherwise objectionable") risk unconstitutional censorship. Agencies should consult First Amendment jurisprudence when defining prohibited categories and procedures for moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation among agencies and the constitutional risk of overbroad or vague moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies vary widely — some delete many categories of comments, some encourage civility without deleting, and some have no policies — raising questions whether particular deletion decisions violate commenters' First Amendment rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example/question: whether a comment that mentions or praises the Confederate States of America qualifies as "otherwise objectionable" or "inciting hate"—this could place an agency at odds with the Fourth Circuit. Guidance: because First Amendment jurisprudence is factually and legally complex, agencies should avoid vague or overbroad terms, enumerate concrete, narrowly tailored standards, and provide transparent procedures to reduce risk of unconstitutional viewpoint or content discrimination.
